body.text: Negotiators at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change in Antalya, Türkiye, entered the scheduled final day on November 20 still divided over a draft agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. Those who worked through the night said they expect the talks to run into Saturday, according to the Associated Press.
Outside, pavilions were being dismantled, and tired delegates crossed the venue in drizzle, Climate Home News reported. Inside, the negotiations were entering their endgame.
“At this point, no one is happy,” Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, told reporters with only hours left before the official close.

The dispute is an old one. Countries agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, but later summits have not made that commitment more specific. The COP30 outcome in Belém, Brazil, last year did not mention fossil fuels at all, which led some countries to pursue exits from coal, oil and gas outside the UN process.

The COP31 presidency released a first draft of the “cover decision”, the overarching political text, on November 16. It ran to 18 pages and 144 paragraphs, and the presidency described it as a compilation of proposals from countries rather than an agreed text. It called for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, CNN reported. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that it also carried a proposal “for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels”.

A second draft, published on Thursday, November 19, runs to nine pages and about 80 paragraphs. It removes both fossil fuel references. It also drops a reference to the voluntary fossil fuel roadmap led by Brazil and a proposal that developed countries reach net zero emissions by 2030, according to RTÉ and the Australian Associated Press.

In their place, the text calls the global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development “irreversible”. It would be the first COP cover decision to say outright that warming is projected to exceed the 1.5°C limit set by the Paris Agreement, Reuters and RTÉ reported. It expresses “deep concern” about the imminent breach, AFP reported, and calls for any overshoot to be kept “as small and short as possible”, according to UN News.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s Climate Change Minister, who chairs the negotiations, said the aim was “finding the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow”. COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s Environment Minister, told reporters: “I do not think we are taking a step back.” He also said the text was not final, Carbon Brief reported.

Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa, said the new text had “gone backwards” from the earlier one and that, if it stood, COP31 would be a “ghost COP”. Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in West Asia and North Africa, said: “[W]eakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining the progress.”
Electrification at the centre

What remains is the “35 by 35” pledge proposed by Türkiye: to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 from just over 20 per cent now. About 75 countries have backed it, Reuters reported, and the EU endorsed it on November 17. The second draft speaks of “global cooperation” towards the goal, a softer formulation than the first draft after developing countries objected to the cost, according to Reuters.

The International Energy Agency (IEA), a strategic partner of the presidency, says reaching 35 per cent would cut importing countries’ annual energy bills by about $400 billion by 2035, and by more than $500 billion at this year’s higher prices.

Interest in electrification has grown since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The Strait of Hormuz crisis has disrupted roughly a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade, according to S&P Global. The European Commission estimates the disruption has added €127 billion to the EU’s energy import bill, Euronews reported.

Critics note that the draft does not require the extra electricity to come from renewable sources, which leaves room for coal and gas plants to count towards the goal, AP reported. In September, Claire Smith of the campaign group Beyond Fossil Fuels warned against electrification becoming a “Trojan horse” for new fossil fuel use. Kurum has argued the opposite: that wider electrification will “automatically” reduce fossil fuel use, Climate Home News reported. “We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” he told AP.

The Arab Group and Russia rejected the earlier text, objecting to language that targets specific energy sources, to top-down sectoral targets and to the 35 per cent goal itself, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin. India has questioned the financial implications of internationally prescribed electrification targets, Climate Current reported.
Carbon capture and methane

The second draft “welcomes” efforts to scale up carbon capture and storage and “recognises” a role for carbon dioxide removal, adding that removal should complement deep emissions cuts and not replace or delay them, Carbon Brief reported.

The campaign group 350.org says one paragraph proposes capturing up to 2.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by 2035, which it puts at 20 to 40 times current capture. Citing Oil Change International, it says almost 80 per cent of carbon capture projects worldwide are used to extract more oil. The Pakistani daily The Express Tribune reported that bracketed targets for carbon storage by 2035 remain in the text, which means they are still contested.

Vanuatu’s Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu told AFP his country was “quite disappointed by the text”. Referring to carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), an expensive and immature technology in the view of its detractors, he said: “We want to see the references to false solutions removed.”

On methane, the draft changes “rapid and substantial reductions” to “reductions” and removes references to specific actions and sectors, except one mention alongside a zero-waste initiative, Carbon Brief reported. AFP also reported that detailed methane reduction methods were dropped.

France had urged countries last week to write near-zero methane emissions intensity for oil and gas by 2030 into the decision, Health Policy Watch reported. The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) says methane emissions must be at least 25 per cent below 2025 levels by 2035 for the world to return to 1.5°C.
Oil deals and objections

On November 19, the day the draft appeared, the leaders of the US, China and Russia met in Shenzhen, China, and agreed to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, according to a joint declaration published by Xinhua. The statement gave no volumes or dates, TT News and Marketplace reported. The US government did not take part directly in the Antalya negotiations, AP reported.

Nana Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators on Climate Change, said countries that advocate climate action while pursuing deals on polluting fuels risk undermining global efforts. “This is a hypocrisy in the whole process,” he told reporters.

Panama has threatened to block any final text that lacks a cap on global oil production, climate finance and an acknowledgement of failing goals, AP reported. Decisions at COPs are taken by consensus, so one country’s formal objection can stall adoption.

Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro told AFP, ahead of talks with the COP31 presidency: “We are very respectful of every opinion and every delegation. And we demand equal respect for our position.” He has also said the talks are “held hostage” by a “petroleum mafia”, according to AP.
‘Fossil COP’ warning

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that the latest draft falls short of the ambition required. “We don’t want this COP to become a ‘fossil’ COP,” the official said. RTÉ quoted an anonymous EU official calling the text “not acceptable and not ambitious enough”.

EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has said the bloc will judge the text on three tests: whether it responds adequately to the climate crisis and the risk of exceeding 1.5°C, whether it implements existing agreements, and whether it reflects the EU’s negotiating mandate, RTÉ reported. He declined to assess the omission of fossil fuel references.

Monique Barbut, France’s Ecological Transition Minister, called the omission a “black mark”. Mary Robinson, a former President of Ireland and a founding member of The Elders, told RTÉ that dropping the reference “undermines the credibility of the whole thing”. The Alliance of Small Island States said COP31 would fail if it did not respond to “out of control warming”, and it wants a specific figure for tripling adaptation finance, the Independent reported.

Some governments are already working outside the UN process. Nearly 60 countries, including some large fossil fuel producers, met in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April for the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels. The next is due in Tuvalu in early 2027, according to the World Resources Institute. Brazil formally presented its own fossil fuel roadmap in Antalya on November 10.
Finance and priorities

Critics have taken aim at the hosts for concentrating on a headline electrification target. “The attempt to prove that a flashy headline target signals success for this COP has gone wrong in many ways,” said Avantika Goswami, programme manager at the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), a research group in India. Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, said: “There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South.”

COP30 agreed to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, which the World Resources Institute calculates as a new target of about $120 billion a year, up from $40 billion. The first COP31 draft wrote that figure in as a floor. The second keeps the pledge to triple but drops the $120 billion figure, and it defers the baseline and the route to delivery to further work, RTÉ reported.

UNEP estimates adaptation needs in developing countries at about $310 billion a year by 2035, against $26 billion in international public adaptation finance in 2023. The deleted $120 billion goal would have covered well under half of that estimate. Developed countries cite budget pressures and say large emerging economies, including China, should contribute more, AFP reported.

The talks follow UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report, published on October 21, which found that the chance of holding warming to 1.5°C with no or limited overshoot “is gone”. Full delivery of national climate plans would limit warming to 2.6°C, it said. To keep the overshoot as small as possible, emissions would need to fall 18 per cent by 2030 and 45 per cent by 2035 from 2025 levels.
The science timetable

Delegates are also divided over when the seventh assessment reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) should appear. The second draft “invites” the panel to present all three working group reports before the second global stocktake, the review of progress under the Paris Agreement that is due to conclude in 2028, Carbon Brief reported.

Dozens of countries want the reports before the stocktake. Saudi Arabia and India, among a smaller group, want them postponed to 2029, AFP reported. Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday that it was “not seeking to delay climate science”, Al Jazeera reported.

At earlier IPCC meetings, Kenya, India, China and South Africa opposed accelerated timelines, citing the time needed for government review and gaps in the research literature, according to Carbon Brief. Both camps cite inclusivity of developing-country scientists in support of their positions.

Trade language was also softened. Concerns about unilateral trade measures are now merely noted, and a call on developed countries to phase such measures out by 2027 was cut, Carbon Brief reported. India and other emerging economies object to measures such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which can raise costs for exporters, Down To Earth reported.
What happens next

Bowen said consultations would continue with every negotiating group, and told reporters: “We won’t be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus.” Reuters said the revised draft was not expected to be the final version. Recent COPs have often run more than 24 hours past their deadlines. The next summit, COP32, is scheduled for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November 2027, according to AP.
For now, the pavilions in Antalya are being packed away while the central question stays open: whether nearly 200 countries will agree on a text, and whether that text will mention fossil fuels.
(with inputs from agencies)
